title: Laser Weapons Will Be Deployed At Cape Canaveral Spaceport To Take Down Drones
body: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station is getting lasers that can zap drones intruding into its airspace. When installed, the new directed energy defense system will be part of a much larger effort to protect the spaceport against drone incursions, a spokesperson for Space Launch Delta 45 (SLD 45) told us. The idea is to ensure the safety of launches and to keep prying eyes away from an installation full of secrets about America’s military and commercial space efforts. Companies like SpaceX, United Launch Alliance, Blue Origin and Relativity Space use the installation for space launches. The base defense modernization effort comes as the Cape Canaveral region is inundated with drone incursions. There were hundreds last year. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, on May 29, 2026. (U.S. Space Force photo by Gwen Kurzen) Gwendolyn Kurzen “As the world’s premier spaceport continues to support an unprecedented launch tempo for national security and commercial missions, securing critical launch infrastructure from low-altitude aerial threats remains a top operational priority,” the spokesperson explained. “The ongoing security modernization integrates detection, tracking, and defensive capabilities to include directed energy systems. These will provide security forces with real-time situational awareness and the necessary tools to safeguard personnel, launch complexes, and national security payloads.” The spokesperson did not have a timeline for when the directed energy system will be operational. Florida Today was the first to report that lasers will make up this defensive system. Col. Brian Chatman, who commands Space Launch Delta 45, told the publication that the facility is “bringing on a directed-energy system that can do a kinetic kill against UASs (Unmanned Aircraft Systems) that are coming into the area that are having nefarious intent.” “The Air Force Research Laboratory [AFRL]-tested system has been proven to be able to safely bring down a drone,” Florida Today noted. “This directed-energy system uses lasers to shoot down any drone that flies into restricted areas.” Chatman didn’t name the specific system to Florida Today and the SLD 45 spokesperson declined to say. The following video shows one such AFRL-tested system that has been used in combat before. For the spaceport, being able to use lasers is even more important than it is for other locations needing protection from drones. That’s because the traditional method of jamming radio frequencies to interfere with drone connections to controllers could damage spacecraft. “If you start blasting a bunch of RF energy you run into potential challenges,” Chatman explained. “You don’t want that.” There is good reason for Chatman to be concerned about drones. The spaceport has been subjected to many unauthorized incursions, the spokesperson told us. However, there were no statistics immediately available on how many or whether they occurred during launches. There were 500 unauthorized drone flights over the adjacent Port Canaveral in 2025, Port Canaveral CEO Capt. John Murray said . In addition, on Sept. 18, a Chinese tourist pleaded guilty to a federal misdemeanor charge after flying a drone in restricted airspace above NASA’s Kennedy Space Center (KSC) in late July. KSC is located across the Banana River from the space station. It is unclear if the new laser system will also protect the skies over KSC. The spokesperson did not immediately know and is checking into it. Cape Canaveral. (Google Earth) That tourist, Xiaodong He, flew a drone that videotaped the installation, according to federal documents . The drone got within 1.56 miles of pad 39B, from where the next crewed lunar flight is expected to launch in 2028. NASA’s Kennedy Space Center pad 39B. (NASA) Encompassing about 25 square miles, Cape Canaveral Space Force Station is a large, unpopulated, open area with a long Atlantic Ocean shoreline. The station’s physical layout allows many vectors for drone incursions, and what’s housed there makes it a logical target for a nefarious actor. The systems being prepared for launch and launched at the sprawling facility are extremely valuable and can take many years to build, costing billions. When they are out on the pad or being transported around, the rockets are massive tubes packed with high explosives that would cause a devastating secondary explosion if struck. Even disrupting launches there due to a successful or even attempted attack could have major national security impacts. Maybe the place that needs them most. Use your imagination with this one. Probably scary how little they have. https://t.co/cBww4vlB9n — Tyler Rogoway (@Aviation_Intel) September 19, 2026 The move to bring directed energy systems to protect the spaceport comes as the military is investing heavily in these systems to counter drones. Late last month, for instance, troops from the Joint Task Force-Southern Border (JTF-SB) employed an Army Multipurpose High Energy Laser (AMP-HEL) system during an operation dubbed Ardent Vanguard. The AMP-HEL was used “to engage and defeat three hostile UAS, determined to be such based on their use in direct support of activities posing a physical threat to U.S. military personnel and CBP [Customs and Border Protection] partners,” according to a media release at the time . The shootdown was part of the U.S. government’s ongoing effort to counter drones being flown by Mexican drug cartels. Joint Task Force – Southern Border personnel used the Army Multipurpose High Energy Laser system to engage and defeat a hostile drone. (U.S. Army Photo by Sgt. Daniel Huerta) Operation Ardent Vanguard The military is seeking to expand its ability to counter drones with directed-energy weapons. In May, the Defense Department and Joint Interagency Task Force 401 selected five installations to participate in a directed-energy counter-unmanned aircraft systems pilot program required by the Fiscal Year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act. “This initiative will accelerate the fielding and evaluation of advanced directed energy capabilities to protect critical infrastructure, military installations and homeland missions,” the Pentagon explained. “The locations were deliberately selected to support rigorous testing and operational assessments across diverse environments and mission sets.” The Pentagon selected two “key southern border installations” for this program: Fort Huachuca, Arizona; and Fort Bliss, Texas. It also tabbed Naval Base Kitsap, Washington; Grand Forks Air Force Base, North Dakota; and Whiteman Air Force Base, Missouri. Though the Pentagon is pressing forward with making directed energy a key part of counter-drone efforts, laser weapons have limitations . These include their short-term magazine depth being limited to how many successive shots they can fire before thermal loads require the system to cool down. Energy supply can also be a limiting factor. Additionally, laser systems don’t function as well in heavy cloud cover and other inclement weather . “We can only shoot down with a laser what we can see,” Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) Brig. Gen. Yaniv Rotem once said about the IDF’s Iron Beam laser defense system, which began downing enemy drones in combat last year. You can see the Iron Beam’s first claimed kills in the following video. A World First — Combat-Proven Laser Defense, Powered by Rafael For the first time in history, high-power laser systems have been used to intercept aerial threats in combat. This unprecedented breakthrough took place during the Swords of Iron War — with Rafael’s advanced… pic.twitter.com/B3D6UdCJvE — Rafael Advanced Defense Systems (@RAFAELdefense) May 28, 2025 At the same time, a laser weapon of this kind is very much a point-defense weapon, with its short range meaning that multiple systems will be needed to provide coverage of a significant area. In some situations, even a single, large military base like Cape Canaveral Space Force Station might require more than one to provide full defensive coverage. In addition, there have been concerns about the safety of the systems and the authorities required to use them in the homeland. These issues came to a head in February , when the U.S. military used AeroVironment’s LOCUST directed energy weapon to shoot down a Customs and Border Protection (CBP) drone over southwest Texas. The friendly fire incident spurred expanded airspace restrictions over the Fort Hancock area that lasted for four months. It also gave credence to the FAA’S concerns about the operational deployment of counter-drone laser weapons along the border. The same system was used to fire at suspected Mexican cartel drones flying across the southern border into Texas two weeks earlier , which resulted in a large airspace closure, general confusion and major headlines. Safety concerns about using directed energy weapons, and especially kinetic ones, to take down drones in the U.S. have been a major factor in why they haven’t been previously used in this role. Almost two years ago, officials at U.S. Northern Command (NORTHCOM), which has coordinating authority for counter-drone efforts in the U.S., said the use of such weapons was not yet on the table . The reason is that they can create dangerous or otherwise serious collateral effects that are less of a concern in a war zone. That the U.S. Space Force is bringing in a laser system to protect some of the nation’s most important and secret military assets is a strong indication that these concerns are being overcome. title: Ukraine destroys record 76 Russian air-defense systems this month, losses analyst says Russia “will never be able to restore”
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine has destroyed a record 76 Russian air-defense systems this month, and September is not over. The tally beats a record that had stood since July 2023 and reflects a systematic Ukrainian campaign to hunt down Russia's air defenses, opening the skies over occupied territory and inside Russia, the analyst Oleksandr Kovalenko said on Telegram. Ukraine is methodically peeling apart Russia's layered air defense, and September has been its worst month yet: 76 systems destroyed, past the 73 lost in July 2023, by Kovalenko's count, with days still to go. It is part of a campaign in which Ukrainian drones and special forces have hunted Russian radars and missile launchers across occupied territory and Crimea, and each one destroyed opens a corridor for the next strike. The record falls with days to spare Kovalenko credited Ukraine's Defense Forces' sustained hunt for Russian anti-air, which he said pays off twice: it clears the defenses that would otherwise stop Ukraine's strikes, making later attacks on occupied territory and on Russia itself more effective. Each kill opens a corridor Ukrainian drone and special-operations units have picked off Pantsir, Tor, Buk, and pieces of S-300 and S-400 systems across occupied territory and Crimea, sometimes several in a single night throughout 2026. As Russia pulls its scarce long-range systems back to guard Moscow, fewer are left to cover occupied Ukraine, widening the openings for the next wave of Ukrainian strikes. Russia cannot replace the losses Over the full-scale war, Kovalenko said, Russia has lost more than 1,673 air-defense systems of every kind, from radars to surface-to-air missiles and self-propelled anti-aircraft guns. That, he argued, is a level Moscow can no longer make good with a defense industry already stretched thin by the war. "Such a quantity of equipment Russia will never be able to restore and compensate," he thinks. He added that this means it would no longer be able to return to the pre-war level of closing the sky, neither technically nor technologically." Read also Ukraine’s jet-drone kill rate just hit 55%. Russia’s answer: $12 billion to make more of them Asked if Ukraine would send troops to defend NATO, Zelenskyy offered something else: know-how to stop drones now reaching its neighbors Combat shows speed alone can’t catch Russia’s jet-powered drones, despite eight Ukrainian makers’ assurances. So why can’t they stop them?

title: 4th FW F-15Es Return From Iran Air War With Mortal Kombat-Themed Nose Art And Drone Kill Markings
body: Ten Seymour Johnson F-15Es returning from the Middle East stopped at RAF Mildenhall, revealing new Mortal Kombat-themed nose art and a combined 45 Shahed drone kill markings. The “flow” of F-15E Strike Eagles returning from deployments to the CENTCOM AOR (Area of Responsibility), where they supported Operation Epic Fury against Iran, continues through UK airbases. After 12 F-15E Strike Eagles belonging to the 366th Fighter Wing (FW) touched down at RAF Lakenheath on their way back to Mountain Home AFB on Sept. 16, 2026, ten Seymour Johnson AFB F-15Es arrived at RAF Mildenhall between Sept. 24 and 25. The latter are the first of a total of 24 Strike Eagles belonging to the 4th FW that deployed to the Middle East between January and March 2026. US ORBAT – Fast-Jets – 03/SEP/2026 #IranWar‌ Update to the slightly more detailed US Orders of Battle for fast-jets in CENTCOM available in case of further conflict with Iran. Due to the fact my list of airframes is over 250, I am not going to list individual airframes here,… pic.twitter.com/LoSf2nMNlj — DefenceGeek (@DefenceGeek) September 3, 2026 Upon their arrival in the UK, the 4th FW jets could be seen sporting a variety of Mortal Kombat-inspired nose art and nicknames, along with some interesting Shahed kill markings and bomb silhouettes. For those who don’t know it yet, Mortal Kombat is a long-running and hugely popular fighting video game franchise born in the early 1990s. The first section of four F-15Es, callsigns TABOR 21-24, was supported by KC-135R CLEAN 63, arrived on Sept. 24 and included the following airframes: TABOR 21 SJ AF 89-0490 “Liu Kang” TABOR 22 SJ AF 87-0181 “Sub Zero” TABOR 23 SJ AF 89-0492 “Kitana” TABOR 24 SJ AF 89-0505 “Scorpion” The second section, arrived on Sept. 26, and included: TABOR 11 SJ AF 90-0229 “Reptile” TABOR 12 SJ AF 89-0478 “Kano” TABOR 13 SJ AF 87-0193 “Cage” TABOR 14 SJ 87-0177 “Smoke” TABOR 15 SJ 88-1704 “Shao Kahn” TABOR 16 SJ 88-1670 “Jax” In order of appearance, “Liu Kang” refers to one of the franchise’s central heroes, a Shaolin monk and martial artist; “Sub-Zero” is the iconic cryomancer ninja known for his ability to manipulate ice; “Kitana” is the Edenian princess who fights with steel war fans; and “Scorpion” is the undead ninja warrior famous for his spear attack and “Get over here!” catchphrase. 89-0490 “Liu Kang” | Source: Stewart Jack 87-0181 “Sub Zero” | Source: Stewart Jack 89-0492 “Kitana” | Source: Stewart Jack 89-0505 “Scorpion” | Source: Stewart Jack Dealing with the second section, it featured “Reptile,” the reptilian ninja associated with invisibility and acid attacks; “Kano,” the ruthless Black Dragon mercenary recognizable by his cybernetic eye; “Cage,” a reference to Johnny Cage, the flamboyant Hollywood action star and martial artist; “Smoke,” the Lin Kuei ninja known for smoke-based attacks; “Shao Kahn,” the powerful emperor of Outworld and one of the series’ best-known villains; and “Jax,” or Jackson Briggs, the Special Forces officer distinguished by his cybernetic arms. 90-0229 “Reptile” | Source: Stewart Jack 87-0193 “Cage” | Source: Stewart Jack 87-0177 “Smoke” | Source: Stewart Jack 88-1704 “Shao Kahn” | Source: Stewart Jack 88-1670 “Jax” | Source: Stewart Jack Nose art and nicknames on Strike Eagles deployed to the Middle East first appeared on the 18 F-15E Strike Eagle jets belonging to the 391st Expeditionary Fighter Squadron returning to Mountain Home AFB from OIR (Operation Inherent Resolve) in April 2019 . Since then, it has become a standard for all the F-15E squadrons deployed to the CENTCOM AOR. Besides the nose art, the F-15Es also sport some interesting Shahed-like kill markings, applied to aircraft credited with Iranian drone shootdowns, along with a wide variety of weapon silhouettes. These include AGM-158 JASSM s (Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles), GBU-39 SDBs (Small Diameter Bombs), and what appear to be AGR-20 APKWS II (Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System II) laser-guided rockets. The latter have increasingly become a weapon of choice for the counter-UAS mission, offering a comparatively inexpensive way to engage drones without expending more costly air-to-air missiles. Integration of the APKWS II onto the F-15E began in May 2025, when images surfaced online showing Strike Eagles from Eglin Air Force Base, Florida, flying in a variety of configurations with LAU-131 rocket launchers. As explained at the time , with six LAU-131 launchers the F-15E can carry 42 laser-guided rockets in addition to its standard loadout of eight air-to-air missiles, a payload that gives the jet significant flexibility in combat and up to 50 opportunities to engage aerial targets even before considering the gun. The counter-UAS configuration was employed extensively in combat by the F-15E Strike Eagles of the 366th Fighter Wing, as shown by the bomb markings carried by the jets returning to their home bases from deployment in the Middle East in July 2025. A big thank you to our contributor and friend Stewart Jack Photography for sending us his photos!

title: Asked if Ukraine would send troops to defend NATO, Zelenskyy offered something else: know-how to stop drones now reaching its neighbors
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine, the country under daily Russian attack, is offering to help defend others from it. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine will share its drone-defense experience with partners facing Russia's hybrid and drone attacks, NATO members and non-members alike, through its "Drone Deal" agreements, according to UNIAN. Russia's hybrid and drone attacks are spreading past Ukraine, to Moldova, Germany, and Romania, and Kyiv is casting itself as the country that knows how to counter them. Asked whether he would send Ukrainian troops to defend NATO members, Zelenskyy instead pointed to the drone agreements, bilateral pacts open to partners in or out of NATO, that pair weapons sales and joint production with the transfer of Ukraine's combat experience. Ukraine had signed such deals with nine countries by early August and is negotiating more than a dozen others, becoming, as its officials put it, "a security provider for Europe." The attacks spread past NATO "Russia will continue hybrid attacks against various countries, and not only NATO members," Zelenskyy said, pointing to drone incursions over Moldova, which belongs to neither NATO nor the EU. Those crossings have become routine: Moldova logged 39 Russian drone incursions in the first eight months of the year, and on 24 September, drones entered both Moldova and Romania as Poland scrambled fighters. Ukraine has offered help, Zelenskyy said, "above all to those countries that help us during the war." The Drone Deal shares experience The Drone Deal agreements cover the sale of drones and missiles and joint production, he added, "but also an exchange of experience." He offered a precedent: "How we sent our specialists to the Middle East, how we helped protect critical infrastructure." Sharing how to defend against drones, he said, is "precisely part of this exchange." Ukraine turns security provider Zelenskyy did not answer the question on whether Ukraine would put troops into NATO countries under attack, steering instead to what Ukraine can already give, its hard-won experience of fighting the very weapons now reaching its neighbors' skies. title: Ukraine’s jet-drone kill rate just hit 55%. Russia’s answer: $12 billion to make more of them
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine's defense forces intercepted 55% of Russia's jet-propelled drones in September—more than 1,500 out of over 2,730 launched—Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in his 26 September evening address. Russia's full-scale aerial campaign has shifted from propeller-driven Shaheds Ukraine learned to shoot down at over 90% to jet-propelled models that fly faster, resist jamming, and often slip past existing defenses. 55% and climbing Zelenskyy said military intelligence had briefed him on Russian weapons production—not just jet Shaheds but other technological systems. The documents detail what Moscow is preparing for next year: the volumes and the financing. "We are preparing our countermeasures, and for every line item there must be a Ukrainian answer," he said. Several effective interceptor prototypes are already in combat. "Interceptors have been identified that can become the main tool of our defense. Production, components—all of this we are scaling up. There will be an answer," Zelenskyy said . The goal is to match the interception rate for regular propeller-driven Shaheds, which exceeds 90%. At 55%, the jet-drone rate is climbing but still leaves nearly half reaching their targets. $12 billion for one category Russia plans to spend $12 billion in 2027 on jet drones and loitering munitions alone, Zelenskyy said. "This concerns not only Ukraine and not only us," he added, warning that multiple intelligence agencies have information Russia wants to expand its war to other countries and regions. He said this is why Ukraine is pushing for stronger sanctions and the Drone Deal format. Ukraine has signed 11 such agreements, the latest with Finland at the UN General Assembly this week, and is preparing a 12th with what Zelenskyy called "a strong country." The warning came as Russia struck a Kyiv data center twice on the morning of 27 September, injuring three people including two children, Zelenskyy wrote . Overnight strikes killed three people in Zaporizhzhia Oblast and one man in Kyiv. In total this week, Russia launched more than 2,200 strike drones, roughly 1,650 aerial bombs, and 38 missiles—a significant share of them ballistic—at Ukraine, he said. Explore further A $50 computer just flew Russia’s newest jet drone into a Ukrainian grain ship—and jamming couldn’t stop it Jet drones are now Russia's main aerial weapon Russia's jet-propelled Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones have become the dominant threat in Russia's aerial campaign against Ukrainian cities. By August, production of jet Geran-4/5 models exceeded that of propeller-driven Geran-2s, according to Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR). Russian factories produce roughly 3,000 jet models per month alongside about 2,800 of the older type. The Geran-5 is technically a drone but functions as a small cruise missile—faster, harder to jam, and increasingly guided by AI and mesh networking that complicate interception. Ukraine's answer has been interceptor drones—cheap, fast enough to chase a Geran, and guided by machine vision. A Ukrainian interceptor recently scored its first kills against jet Gerans and is heading into mass production, though a presidential adviser warned that speed alone cannot catch them—machine vision and automatic guidance decide the chase.
